prime.problem: A research question that sounds good can still be unanswerable: already published, too rare to measure, or tested by a design with no power. Without checking each of these cheaply first, you spend the budget and the weeks and learn nothing.
prime.fits: The first step of the capstone. It reuses the power formula from How many runs do you need? and the 21,438-run pilot from Lab: audit 21,000 public runs, and hands the sharpened question to the design cards that follow.
expect: a novelty check you re-run, not a one-off
power as a reason to kill a design
base rate in the wild vs in a forced setting
a two-part paper: decomposition plus causal test
the question as one sentence plus a 'what's new' sentence
prime.goal: Say the paper's question and what's new about it in two sentences, and name the measurement (with its number) that killed each earlier version.

attend: Which earlier version was killed by prior work, which by power, and which by a base rate?
Why does a 0.17% population rate make the controlled study need a forced failing state rather than more tasks?
What does Silence Is Endorsement already show, and which three things does this paper add on top of it?
Why is the 21,438-run pilot half of the paper instead of a failed precursor?
What made the baseline move the story from false claims toward tampering, and why is that still only a lead?

must: A question is only worth running if it is new → the v0 question (do agents falsely claim success?) was already answered by 2606.09863 and SpecHarness → the paper had to name a cause, compaction, that only an anecdote (2607.13071) had touched

Power depends on the baseline rate and the clustering → 30 tasks × 3 repeats at a 20% baseline detects only a 22–27 point jump (21–27% power for 10 points) → v1 would likely miss a realistic effect, so it was resized before any money was spent

Genuine self-contradiction is 0.17% of public claims while honest misses are 15.6% → a doubling from 0.17% needs about 5,110 tasks, from 5% about 160 → the causal test must force the failing state and measure its own dose-0 baseline

Each narrowing was chosen after seeing data → that is a researcher degree of freedom → the analysis is registered before the sweep and every later change is a dated addendum, so the confirmatory result can't be shaped by the pilot
elevated: The novelty script marks ids already in the verified check → only NEW? titles need reading → a weekly re-check costs minutes, which is why the spec can require one before the sweep and another before writing
reference: pilot counts: 8,418 claims, 426 strict, 105 task-relevant, 14 genuine, 1,310 honest misses, 3,092 untested
the arXiv API endpoint export.arxiv.org/api/query with sortBy=submittedDate
Silence Is Endorsement's example: 5% → 60% approvals on Llama-3.1-8B

compress.prompt: Card closed: write the five versions of the question as a chain, one line each, with the measurement and number that ended each one.
checklist: v0 already done (2606.09863 definition; SpecHarness gap)
v1 underpowered: detects 22–27 points, 21–27% power at 10
v2: compaction never fired in the smoke test; genuine self-contradiction 0.17% in 21,438 runs
v3: decomposition of the gap plus a causal test from a forced failing state
v4: unfixable test, branching, pre-registration; baseline P1 near zero, tampering +20 points (exploratory)

retrieve.q: Explain the difference between the paper's 'what's new' claim and the gap Silence Is Endorsement already filled.
answer: Silence Is Endorsement: summarizers drop the 'unverified' status of authorization claims, and a separate monitor then approves risky actions
this paper: test status in coding agents, the agent's own final claim, checked against the repo
plus a dose-response design across transplanted harness prompts, paired and pre-registered

retrieve.q: Walk through how the 0.17% figure changed the controlled experiment's design.
answer: at 0.17% a doubling needs about 5,110 tasks: unaffordable
so the study forces every run into a failing state (an unfixable test)
the baseline becomes the dose-0 rate in that state, measured by the baseline pilot
n is then sized from that rate, not from the population rate

retrieve.q: Forcing the failing state buys power. What does it cost in realism, and how does the paper pay for it?
answer: an always-failing integration test is constructed, not natural; the instruction becomes unsatisfiable as stated
it may push agents toward tampering more than real repos would
the paper pairs it with the 21,438-run observational decomposition and states the limitation

retrieve.q: What does the novelty script do with an id it doesn't recognise, and what must you do next?
answer: it prints NEW? beside the title
you read the title; anything about compaction, summaries or success claims gets its abstract read
you cite it or rule it out in a note, before the sweep and again before writing

compare.q: The pilot lab ended with 'the hypothesis fails'. This card treats the same result as half the paper. What changed between the two readings?
answer: the lab tested whether natural self-contradiction is common enough to study: it isn't
the card reframes the same data as an answer to a different question: where the claim–pass gap comes from
the failed hypothesis also fixed the causal design: force the state, measure its own baseline

compare.q: The power card computed what 30 × 3 could detect. Which of its inputs turned out wrong for this paper, and in which direction?
answer: the 20% baseline was far too high for natural self-contradiction (0.17%)
ρ 0.2–0.5 was too high for self-contradiction (pilot ρ 0.055) but right in spirit for honest misses (0.32)
lesson: the baseline drives n; measure it before committing

predict.q: Suppose the sweep finds tampering does not rise after compaction (a null), and P1 stays near zero. Before reading the next cards, predict which parts of the paper still stand.
predict.answer: The 21,438-run decomposition stands on its own: it is new regardless of the sweep. A tight null on P1, P2 and tampering is the first controlled measurement and bounds the effect (the baseline pilot expects an upper interval near +5 points on P1). What falls is the headline 'compaction changes what agents do to tests', so the title and abstract change; the design, the registration and the release don't.

apply.task: Run python3 code/the-question.py 'abs:"reward hacking" AND abs:"coding agent"', a query aimed at the tampering angle. For each NEW? hit, decide from the title whether it needs an abstract read, and write one line saying why.
apply.done: You have a dated list of the NEW? ids for that query, each marked 'read abstract' or 'off-topic' with a reason. On 2026-10-01 the query returned six hits, one of them known (2608.29460, the escalation-channels paper) and five NEW?, of which at least one (a 'RECEIPT' paper whose title says it is reward-hacking-resistant) is close enough to need an abstract read.
apply.hint: Titles about verifying the agent's work or resisting reward hacking are the ones a reviewer would ask about; DNA or game titles are noise from keyword matching.

reflect: Which prediction did you get wrong: that v0 was already published, or that the natural rate would be so low?
What couldn't you explain cleanly: why power kills v1, or why a forced state fixes v2?
Which relationship is still fuzzy: base rate → number of tasks, or researcher choices → why pre-registration comes next?
Which piece of prior work would a reviewer most likely say you missed, and how would you check?
If you had to cut one of the paper's two parts, which would you keep, and why?
